Surgical removal of mature ovarian teratomas is indicated for large, symptomatic masses, those growing in size or if malignancy is suspected. C

background.definition: Ovarian teratomas are a type of germ cell tumor that arises from the primordial germ cells of the ovary (i.e., ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm) and may be of mature or immature morphology .

list.listitem: Annual incidence of benign ovarian teratoma was 8.9/100,000 women in the United Kingdom. The age-specific incidence is highest from age 20 to 50 years and drops off around the time of menopause.
Ovarian teratomas comprise up to 25% of ovarian neoplasms with approximately 5% being malignant; the latter primarily occurring in women from age 16 to 20 years.
In the US, malignant ovarian teratomas occur more frequently among Hispanic women and Pacific Islanders compared to non-Hispanic White and non-Hispanic Black women.
Age-adjusted incidence per 100,000 woman-years is 0.120 for immature teratoma and 0.011 for teratoma with malignant degeneration.
Mature teratoma represented 26% to 44% of primary ovarian neoplasms, depending on the population studied.

In a case series of 222 patients who were 20 years or younger with 235 ovarian lesions detected by computed tomography (CT), 160 (68.1%) were tumors of which 71 were mature teratomas and 7 were immature teratomas.
Bilateral mature teratomas are present in 10% to 17% of cases.

The rate of malignant transformation of mature teratomas was reported to be 0.2% in a case series of 24,092 patients, with squamous cell carcinoma being the most common pathologic finding. Smaller case series have reported similar rates of malignant transformation.
Ovarian teratomas are a type of germ cell tumor that arises from the primordial germ cells of the ovary. They include ectodermal, mesodermal, and endodermal elements.
Mature teratomas are composed of differentiated elements (e.g., skin, hair, teeth) and are referred to as dermoid cysts.
Immature teratomas are composed of poorly differentiated elements from the three cell layers.
Symptoms are primarily from local mass effect or ovarian torsion, although malignant transformation and metastatic disease can occur.

Anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) encephalitis is a rare complication associated with teratomas; it occurs when neural components of the teratoma trigger the formation of antibodies against NMDAR.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Late menarche, fewer pregnancies, infertility, alcohol excess, higher socioeconomic status and higher levels of education.

list.listitem: TVUS is the recommended initial imaging study for evaluation of ovarian masses. Most imaged teratomas have the classic dermoid cyst appearance whether they are benign or malignant. C

Advanced imaging, such as computerized tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), can further characterize lesions over an ultrasound, but their utility is still limited in ruling out malignancy. C

In postmenopausal women with a CA-125 level greater than 35 U/mL, a pelvic mass should be treated as malignant. A CA-125 greater than 200 U/mL should prompt concern for malignancy in premenopausal women; however, this threshold is based on expert opinion and observational data. C

list.listitem: Abdominal pain, increased pelvic pressure, and/or a palpable abdominal mass may be present.
A significant portion of patients are asymptomatic, and the ovarian mass is found incidentally on physical exam or imaging.
Pelvic examination has been shown to have low sensitivity for detection of adnexal masses and performance is worse when subjects are obese.

TVUS is the recommended initial imaging study for evaluation of ovarian masses. In cases of suspected adnexal mass in postmenopausal women, the American College of Radiology (ACR, 2023) notes that magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) without contrast or MRI without and with contrast may be appropriate as initial imaging.

Most imaged teratomas have the classic dermoid cyst appearance whether they are benign or malignant. However, on imaging benign solid tumor components can be difficult to distinguish from imaging findings typically found in malignant masses.

Mature teratomas classically present as a dermoid cyst on imaging; there is a stereotypical appearance on ultrasound. TVUS was 94% sensitive and 98% specific (LR+ 47, LR- 0.06) for the diagnosis of mature teratoma in a series of 329 consecutive patients with adnexal mass.
Immature teratomas are described as having solid and cystic components on imaging with scattered calcifications.

In the case series of young patients noted above, mature teratoma presented as a cystic mass with bulk fat and coarse calcification, and immature teratoma presented as a solid mass with foci of fat and fine calcification.
A retrospective review of 188 ovarian teratomas did not identify any ultrasound characteristics that could definitively rule out malignancy.
In cases of adnexal mass that is highly suspicious for malignancy, ACR recommends CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast or MRI without and with IV contrast as the initial follow-up study.

A retrospective review of 11 patients with teratomas found that the following characteristics seen on MRI or CT were associated with malignant transformation: larger than 9.9 cm of the largest diameter, the presence of enhancing soft tissue components, an obtuse angle between the soft tissue components and the inner wall of the cyst, as well as extracapsular tumor growth with extension into adjacent structures or disseminated metastasis.

A retrospective review of 23 patients aged 45 years and older with teratomas at least 10 cm in diameter revealed the following CT characteristics that were significantly associated with malignant transformation: nodular formation of the soft tissue component, enhancement of the soft tissue component, and an obtuse angle between the soft tissue components and the inner wall of the cyst.
A retrospective study of 117 patients with benign teratomas found that 19% had enhancing solid components on MRI.

Among 138 children with primary ovarian tumors, mixed cystic and solid appearance with or without calcification was seen in 83.5% of pediatric ovarian malignant germ cell tumors; associated benign teratoma was common.

In a retrospective study of 28 patients with teratoma who underwent positron emission tomography (PET)/CT, a maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax) cut-off of 3.6 was 100% sensitive and 81% specific in distinguishing malignant from benign teratomas. However, another retrospective study of 34 patients found an SUVmax cutoff of 2.8 to be only 91% sensitive and 91% specific for distinguishing malignant and benign teratomas.

After menopause, the incidence of benign teratoma decreases and the incidence of ovarian cancer increases. Therefore, in post-menopausal women, CA-125 should be used to further quantify risk of malignancy. A CA-125 level greater than 35 U/mL in a postmenopausal woman with a pelvic mass should be treated as malignant.

The tumor marker CA-125 has a high false positive rate in younger premenopausal women, due to the low cancer prevalence in the population and numerous benign gynecologic conditions that can elevate CA-125. It is suggested that levels of CA-125 >200 U/mL should prompt concern for malignancy in premenopausal women, although this threshold is based on expert opinion and observational data.
There is no current consensus on the role of biomarkers in premenopausal women when imaging suggests mature teratoma.

Multiple studies have observed elevated tumor markers in mature teratoma, with CA-19-9 being the most consistently elevated (Table 1). However, the usefulness of CA-19-9 in prospectively distinguishing benign teratoma from malignancy is undetermined.
In a patient with pelvic pain, pelvic pressure, or an abdominal mass palpated on exam, use TVUS as the initial imaging test.

In a premenopausal woman, if the mass shows classic findings for a mature teratoma on imaging (dermoid cyst), consider expectant management with serial ultrasound. Proceed to surgical removal if symptoms develop, the mass shows rapid growth, or if patient prefers surgical intervention.
If the patient is postmenopausal, or if there is concern for malignancy on imaging, check CA-125 and other serum biomarkers to help further stratify risk of malignancy.
In a postmenopausal patient with benign findings on imaging and normal CA-125, proceed to surgical removal of the mass.
If characteristics on imaging or CA-125 suggest malignancy, involve a gynecologic oncologist in management prior to surgical intervention.
If the mass is poorly visualized on ultrasound, or if there is concern for malignancy, follow up with CT or MRI to help with pre-operative surgical planning.
Surgical removal of mature ovarian teratomas is indicated for large, symptomatic masses, those growing in size or if malignancy is suspected. C
Surgical removal is first-line treatment for immature teratomas. C
Laparoscopy is preferred over laparotomy for mature teratoma due to decreased complications of surgery and similar rates of recurrence. A
Adjuvant platinum-based chemotherapy is used for treatment of immature teratomas and teratomas with malignant degeneration, although impact on outcomes is unclear. C
Expectant management with serial ultrasound is a reasonable alternative for asymptomatic tumors with benign characteristics on imaging. B
Chemotherapy is not recommended for mature teratomas without malignant transformation.
The role of chemotherapy is unclear in teratomas with malignant transformation. If used, platinum-based therapies are most common.
Chemotherapy is not recommended for immature teratomas that are stage I, grade 1 tumors based on low recurrence rates after surgical treatment.
Post-operative chemotherapy is the standard of care for adults with immature teratoma other than stage I, grade 1, although impact on recurrence rates is unclear.
In children, post-operative chemotherapy is not recommended for immature teratoma regardless of stage and grade.
Surgical removal is the primary treatment for mature and immature teratomas.
Laparoscopic surgery appears effective with only a 0.2% incidence of chemical peritonitis.
In women with mature teratoma, laparoscopic surgery is associated with decreased pain, decreased need for analgesia, a shorter recovery period, and a shorter hospital stay compared with laparotomy.
In women with mature teratoma treated with cystectomy, it is unclear whether laparoscopy has an increased rate of recurrence compared with laparotomy at 2 to 5 years of follow-up.

In women with mature teratoma, conversion from laparoscopy to laparotomy occurred in 11% of cases, largely due to size of the teratoma. Lower rates of conversion were reported in studies where cyst size was limited to ≤10 cm and ≤12 cm.

In women undergoing surgery for benign ovarian tumors, laparoscopy was associated with a reduction in fever, postoperative complication, postoperative pain, number of days in the hospital, and total cost compared with laparotomy.

To date, there are no large studies directly comparing cystectomy with oophorectomy regarding outcomes or recurrence rate. However, a retrospective review of 43 subjects with immature teratomas who underwent either ovarian cystectomy or unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy found no statistically significant differences in survival or fertility outcomes.
In a series of planned laparoscopic cystectomies for benign ovarian cysts, 1.6% were converted to oophorectomy.
No studies directly compare surgical treatment with expectant management of mature teratoma.

In a cohort of premenopausal women with adnexal masses less than 6 cm in diameter and with benign ultrasound characteristics who were expectantly managed for an average of 40 months, there were no complications and no diagnoses of ovarian cancer.

In a cohort of women with an ultrasound diagnosis of mature teratoma who were managed expectantly; 31% had surgery within 5 years. The ovarian torsion rate was 0.2% and no cases of malignancy were diagnosed.
Immature teratomas are difficult to distinguish from malignant ovarian tumors based on imaging and should not be expectantly managed.
Anti-NMDAR encephalitis is treated with immunotherapy and tumor removal.

For this problem, first-line immunotherapy consists of steroids, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), and plasma exchange, either alone or in combination. This results in remission of symptoms in about 50% of patients.

Second-line immunotherapy for anti-NMDAR encephalitis consists of rituximab or cyclophosphamide alone or in combination. This resulted in remission of symptoms in 78% of patients who had failed first-line immunotherapy.
In patients who failed first-line immunotherapy, second-line immunotherapy was associated with better outcomes compared with additional first-line immunotherapy or no additional therapy.
In the case of suspected ovarian torsion, emergent surgery is indicated to return circulation to the ovary.
Mature teratomas have a good prognosis after surgical removal with low recurrence rates. B
Ovarian tumors diagnosed during pregnancy have a low risk of malignancy. If they have benign characteristics on imaging, they can be observed until the post-partum period. B
Mature teratomas are expected to grow at 1.7 mm to 1.8 mm per year, although this may be slower in post-menopausal women.
Mature teratoma carries a good prognosis; 2-year recurrence rates of 0% to 7% have been reported.

In children, extracranial mature and immature teratomas have a good prognosis with 5-year survival rates of 99% and 95% respectively. Complete resection and gonadal location are associated with improved survival rates.
Conservative (ovary-sparing) surgical treatment of immature teratomas combined with chemotherapy had a 98% 5-year survival rate and good fertility outcomes.
In teratomas with malignant transformation, 93% 5-year survival was reported if the tumor was confined to the ovary; survival rates were much worse with tumors spread outside the ovary.

Benign ovarian tumors were diagnosed in 0.03% of pregnancies in an Israeli population. Of these, 37% were mature teratomas. Of patients with cysts, 3% underwent ovarian torsion during pregnancy, suggesting that benign appearing ovarian lesions can be managed expectantly until the postpartum period.
Ovarian tumors were discovered in 0.2% of pregnancies delivered at a teaching hospital; 39% were benign teratomas.

An adnexal mass >5 cm was diagnosed in 0.05% of a series of 127,177 pregnant patients. Of these, 6% required surgery prior to delivery for suspected torsion and 20% had antepartum surgery due to characteristics concerning for malignancy on imaging. The remaining patients were observed until cesarean or postpartum period, and all had benign tumors on pathology suggesting that observation until the postpartum period is appropriate for tumors with benign characteristic in imaging.
